{"id": "87:12/q08", "question": "What fate in the Fire is described with this verse and the next?", "turns_on": "The Prophetic report distinguishes permanent inhabitants from those God later removes.", "positions": [{"id": "87:12/q08/p1", "position": "Those destined to remain suffer without death, relief, or a life worth calling life.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī says there is neither death for relief nor beneficial life. Ibn Kathīr reports the Prophet's distinction and connects enduring torment to 43:77 and 35:36, which say its inhabitants are not killed and punishment is not eased. Iṣlāḥī says evaders who deny the Hereafter face eternal fire and will wish vainly for death; Kur'an Yolu says continued existence amid horrific suffering is no positive life. Ibn Kathīr adds that the person remains conscious of painful punishment."}, {"id": "87:12/q08/p2", "position": "Those whom God removes from Hell become charcoal, emerge in groups, and sprout by Paradise's rivers.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports the Prophet's distinction between these people and those destined to remain in Hell."}]}
{"id": "87:12/q09", "question": "How does the fire warning connect with the surrounding verses?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize different links: contrasting responses and fates, reciprocal ellipsis, or clarification of the earlier label.", "positions": [{"id": "87:12/q09/p1", "position": "It gives the bad outcome of evading the reminder, balanced by the good outcome promised to those who heed it.", "reasons": "Qutb says the Prophet's duty is to remind, after which people diverge by their reception. Iṣlāḥī says the fearful heed the warning while the obdurate evade it; the messenger should not force them. Corpus Coranicum sees verses 10–11's responses matched with fates in verses 12–15, a chiasm comparable to 92:5–11 and 92:14–21, with the warning balanced by the promise in 87:14–15."}, {"id": "87:12/q09/p2", "position": "The passage uses paired omissions: the causes and outcomes of the two groups imply their unspoken opposites.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says fear and happiness imply the other's omitted hardness and misery; the misery named as cause implies omitted happiness. Al-Malawī says Quranic concision pairs cause and consequence across passages, likening judgment, decree, and ordainment to designing a waterwheel, constructing it, and measuring its water. Al-Biqāʿī also pairs the fire with its omitted opposite and later purification with its omitted opposite; purification, remembrance, and prayer form a therapy sequence, reprise 87:1's removal of defects and acquisition of perfections, and link prayer with escape from the fire."}, {"id": "87:12/q09/p3", "position": "The explicit burning explains the previously vague description 'most wretched.'", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr relates this clarification to the early Meccan setting."}]}
{"id": "87:12/q10", "question": "How does this warning fit the surah's broader message?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:12/q10/p1", "position": "It makes revelation's public admonition part of a surah about divine praise, the messenger's mission, and afterlife recompense.", "reasons": "Qutb describes the cosmos praising God and the Prophet receiving good news of preservation and ease; he names oneness in creation, revelation, and afterlife recompense as foundations rooted in earlier scriptures (87:18–19), alongside the ease of the message, messenger, and community. Corpus Coranicum says the second stanza addresses the messenger again: after praising God, perhaps with close followers, he speaks to a wider audience, making the revelation of verse 6 public in purpose."}]}
{"id": "87:12/q11", "question": "How does the next surah relate to this fire warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:12/q11/p1", "position": "Al-Ghāshiyah elaborates the same warning and the same great punishment.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī identifies this passage's great Fire with al-Ghāshiyah's great torment, citing 88:21–26."}]}
{"id": "87:12/q12", "question": "What are the surah's setting, length, and recitational associations?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:12/q12/p1", "position": "It is Meccan, has nineteen verses, and was beloved to the Prophet, who recited it with al-Ghāshiyah at Eid and Friday prayers.", "reasons": "Qutb says the two surahs were sometimes recited on the same day and cites 88:1."}]}
{"id": "87:14/q01", "question": "What does aflaha promise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:14/q01/p1", "position": "Attaining one's desired good and lasting felicity, including salvation and Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Ibn Jawzī explain enduring life and success; Wāḥidī specifies lasting residence in Paradise. Al-Ālūsī and Bursawī pair escape from feared harm with attainment of hoped-for good. Jishumī calls falāḥ attainment of one's goal; Ibn ʿĀshūr includes both victory and benefit, citing 2:5. Biqāʿī says every desired good; Quṭb distinguishes worldly sweetness of remembrance from afterlife rescue and bliss."}]}
{"id": "87:14/q02", "question": "Why use qad and the perfect tense for success?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:14/q02/p1", "position": "They present the promised success as certain and announce good news after the warning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 23:1 and 91:9 and says the wording encourages the wicked hearers to join those who fear God. Bursawī says qad prepares listeners for the good outcome and answers an implied question about the rememberer."}]}
{"id": "87:14/q03", "question": "What does the form tazakkā convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:14/q03/p1", "position": "It conveys deliberate effort to become pure and cultivate the self.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr derives striving from the tafaʿʿala form, compares the purification and corruption of 91:9–10, and says the process begins with monotheism and includes good works and almsgiving. Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes cultivating the self toward good."}]}
{"id": "87:14/q04", "question": "Why name the purifier where the rememberer might be expected?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "87:14/q04/p1", "position": "The wording describes the rememberer by the prior trait of purification.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the expected expression would identify the one who remembers; naming the purifier instead characterizes that person by the state that precedes remembrance."}]}
{"id": "87:14/q05", "question": "What purification does tazakkā describe?", "turns_on": "Whether purification is understood as faith, moral and ritual cleansing, growth in virtue, charity generally, or the specifically later fiṭra rite; arguments invoke word usage, context, cross-references, reports, and chronology.", "positions": [{"id": "87:14/q05/p1", "position": "Leaving idolatry or unbelief through faith and professing God's oneness.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, ʿAṭāʾ and others identify confession of no deity but God; the report through Jābir adds rejection of idols and affirming Muhammad's mission. Rāzī prefers this: the omitted object comes from the preceding warning, and cleansing unbelief is purification's fullest instance. Ibn Jawzī and Thaʿlabī appeal to the sūra's Meccan setting."}, {"id": "87:14/q05/p2", "position": "Cleansing the self broadly from sins, corrupt traits, and worldly attachment while obeying God.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī joins avoidance of disbelief and sin to commands and obligations. Kashshāf and Bayḍāwī include sins with unbelief; Ibn Kathīr mentions base traits and following revelation. Biqāʿī extends cleansing to belief, character, speech, acts and wealth. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses worldly attachment and uses ablution as an illustration. Elmalılı includes heart, body, sincerity, ritual washing and charity; Qutb says every stain. Qatāda explicitly allows purification of wealth or of character."}, {"id": "87:14/q05/p3", "position": "Doing righteous deeds and practicing scrupulous piety.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and al-Rabīʿ describe deeds as pure, sound and growing; Qatāda also mentions waraʿ. Wāḥidī says many good works, and the Wajīz combines these with Paradise. The Study Quran calls this purification through good deeds."}, {"id": "87:14/q05/p4", "position": "Increasing or growing in piety, fear of God, and goodness.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj derives this from zakī, 'growing and abundant'; Kashshāf and Bayḍāwī likewise cite zakā as growth. Rāzī adduces believers' success at 23:1–2 and the God-conscious at 2:5. Māwardī allows increase in goodness and righteousness."}, {"id": "87:14/q05/p5", "position": "Purifying oneself in preparation for prayer.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī and Ālūsī present this as a possible sense; Bursawī's variant has the person repent, hear the prayer call, then go to pray."}, {"id": "87:14/q05/p6", "position": "Giving charitable alms from one's wealth, including general charity.", "reasons": "Abū al-Aḥwaṣ urges even a small gift before prayer and sometimes two units afterward; Ibn Masʿūd applies the sequence to giving before setting out for prayer. Ibn ʿAbbās, asked about fiṭra, says he heard no such restriction and means all zakāt and then all charities. Qatāda says wealth-giving pleases the Creator; Nasafī compares the verb to tasaddaqa."}, {"id": "87:14/q05/p7", "position": "Paying all obligatory alms due on property.", "reasons": "This is explicit in Ṭabarī's 'others,' Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, Māwardī, Ibn Jawzī and Qurṭubī; ʿAṭāʾ rejects a restriction to fiṭr. Muqātil and Rāzī join obligatory alms with the regular prayers. Kuran Yolu says early Meccan financial duties need not be the later formal institution, citing 51:19, 70:24 and 9:103."}, {"id": "87:14/q05/p8", "position": "Paying the charity of breaking the fast before Eid prayer.", "reasons": "Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib, Abū Saʿīd, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū al-ʿĀliya, Ibn Sīrīn and others apply the verse to fiṭra; variants place payment before setting out, at the prayer ground, or early Eid morning. Abū al-ʿĀliya says Medinans valued it w

{"id": "87:14/q06", "question": "Who is the successful person in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether man is read as a general description or linked by particular reports to ʿUthmān or Abū Bakr.", "positions": [{"id": "87:14/q06/p1", "position": "Any person who purifies himself and responds to God's reminder.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies this person with the one who fears and remembers in 87:9–10; Corpus Coranicum says the messenger exemplifies a general appeal to believers. Other commentators describe a general pattern of belief, worship and charitable action."}, {"id": "87:14/q06/p2", "position": "ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān.", "reasons": "A report through ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās says ʿUthmān gave an orchard in exchange for a hypocrite's leaning palm whose fallen dates fed an Anṣārī family, after the hypocrite refused the Prophet's promise of a tree in Paradise; 87:11 concerns that hypocrite. Qurṭubī gives no grading."}, {"id": "87:14/q06/p3", "position": "Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk reports that the sūra or verse came down concerning him."}]}
{"id": "87:14/q07", "question": "How does purification lead into remembrance and prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the sequence expresses a spiritual progression, the timing of charity and prayer, or their combined effect.", "positions": [{"id": "87:14/q07/p1", "position": "Purification is the foundation; remembrance brings knowledge of God and prayer expresses obedience.", "reasons": "Rāzī, Bursawī and Ibn ʿĀshūr order the stages as clearing false belief, knowing or recalling God's names and perfections with fear and hope, then bodily service. Ibn ʿĀshūr says a pure soul accepts guidance and cites 29:45; the Study Quran adds heart, tongue and action."}, {"id": "87:14/q07/p2", "position": "The sequence can describe almsgiving before prayer, especially fiṭra before Eid prayer.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd and Abū al-Aḥwaṣ apply the order to giving before prayer; Ibn ʿUmar checks charity before leaving for Eid. Qutb describes a living bond with God here and bliss hereafter."}]}
{"id": "87:14/q08", "question": "What does the verse teach about the path to success?", "turns_on": "The notes vary in whether they emphasize faith and outward practice, inward discipline, or detachment from worldly desire.", "positions": [{"id": "87:14/q08/p1", "position": "Success follows purification, remembrance and prayer, with faith and obedient deeds.", "reasons": "Muqātil names testimony, alms and five prayers; Jishumī combines obligations with avoidance of grave sins and says the actions are human acts. Abū Ḥayyān joins worship and charity. These distinguish the sura's opening from its later verses."}, {"id": "87:14/q09/p2", "position": "The sūra is Meccan, so its original reference cannot require Eid or fiṭra, which did not yet exist there.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī calls the Meccan dating a consensus; Ibn Jawzī prefers Ibn ʿAbbās's faith reading. {"id": "87:14/q10", "question": "How does this promise relate to the sūra's warning and opening?", "turns_on": "Which part of the sūra or other verse is taken as the key to this promise: the immediate warning, the opening command, or parallel accounts of purification and success.", "positions": [{"id": "87:14/q10/p1", "position": "It balances the warning about the most wretched with the reward of those who fear, heed the reminder and purify themselves.", "reasons": "Muqātil contrasts Meccan unbelievers who neither purify nor pray. Rāzī supplies unbelief as purification's object from the warning. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the verse a resumption after punishment and identifies the purified with those who fear and remember. Corpus Coranicum describes a balance, and a chiasm between responses in 10–11 and outcomes in 12–15, comparing 92:5–11 and 14–21; it says the reminder's implied content includes fear, purification, invocation and prayer."}, {"id": "87:14/q10/p2", "position": "Purification and prayer reprise the opening command to glorify God and complete its account of guidance.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī sees paired omissions: fear implies its opposite and misery implies happiness; fire's opposite and purification's opposite are likewise implied. Corpus Coranicum sees verse 15 recalling the opening's Creator praise and the public aim of verse 6's revelation."}, {"id": "87:14/q10/p3", "position": "The purification here is linked to similar Qurʾānic statements about succeeding through piety and self-purification.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 23:1–2 and 2:5 for success of humble believers and the God-conscious. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 91:9–10 for purified versus corrupted souls; Corpus Coranicum sends readers to 91:9. Al-Intiṣāf's author cites 87:14 to support God as subject of purification at 91:5, keeping oath pronouns consistent and reading purification as a passive-like result."}, {"id": "87:14/q10/p4", "position": "The wider sūra frames revelation, divine unity, and afterlife recompense as a message to the messenger and wider audience.", "reasons": "Qutb says the Prophet loved this nineteen-verse Meccan sūra and recited it with al-Ghāshiya at Eid and Friday prayers; its cosmos praises God and its revelation promises preservation and ease. Corpus Coranicum says the messenger's address can be exemplary for believers; the social ethic implied in purification is less explicit than Q 90 and Q 107."}]}

{"id": "87:15/q03", "question": "What prayer does 'then prayed' denote?", "turns_on": "Whether ṣallā names the later prescribed cycle, Eid, voluntary prayer, supplication, or earlier/broader worship.", "positions": [{"id": "87:15/q03/p1", "position": "The five prescribed daily prayers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās repeatedly supplies this gloss; the Jābir report adds keeping them at their appointed times. {"id": "87:15/q04", "question": "How does remembrance relate in time to prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether the coordinating fāʾ enforces chronological sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "87:15/q04/p1", "position": "Remembrance precedes and prompts prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says reversing the conjunction's order violates normal syntax. Ibn ʿĀshūr says recollection naturally produces reverence and prayer."}, {"id": "87:15/q04/p2", "position": "The wording need not impose the actual order; prayer can precede or contain remembrance.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī illustrates with visiting and honoring in either verbal order. {"id": "87:15/q13", "question": "What variant pronunciations affect words in this verse?", "turns_on": "The reported difference between verse-final and internal lām, and the noun's first vowel.", "positions": [{"id": "87:15/q13/p1", "position": "The final lām in fa-ṣallā may be softened at verse end, while nonfinal counterparts are pronounced emphatically.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī cites this preferred distinction for euphony against a preceding emphatic trigger; verse-final examples are 75:31, 87:15 and 96:10, contrasted with nonfinal yaslā at 87:12."}, {"id": "87:15/q13/p2", "position": "The noun for remembrance is pronounced with either kasra or ḍamma on its first consonant.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī records the two pronunciations."}]}
